To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
JEV infection of mouse brains leads to the induction of 23 genes, including GARG39, and that GARG39 is a microtubular associated protein.

1) JEV infection of the brain activates a large number of genes that are not induced by Sindbis infection; 2) JEV and Sindbis infection activate a number of common host genes; 3) GARG39 protein has been identified as a novel microtubule-binding protein.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of host genes that respond to viral infection, with a focus on those that are induced by neurotropic flaviviruses and the characterization of the function of one such gene, GARG39/ISG54/MuP54.
the identification of novel host factors which are induced during viral infections and may play an important role in the viral life cycle.
the identification of host factors involved in the replication and/or pathogenesis of JEV, which could be exploited as novel targets for antiviral drug discovery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the identification of novel JEV-inducable genes, including GARG39, provides new insights into the molecular basis of JEV infection.
GARG39 is a microtubular protein, whose expression is induced by a variety of viral infections and whose expression is regulated by a number of different stimuli, including glucocorticoids.
GARG39 has been identified as a novel microtubule-binding protein that interacts with tubulins and is enriched in mitotic spindles of dividing cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
JEV infection induces the expression of a large number of genes, many of which are common to Sindbis virus, and that the JEV-inducable gene IFIT2/GARG39 is a microtubules-associated protein.
JEV infection of the mouse brain induces expression of a number of genes which have not previously been shown to be regulated by any other neurovirulent virus.

the study of viral infections can be an effective tool to identify new genes and their functions in the mammalian brain, as well as provide a new insight into the pathogenesis and host response to viral infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
GARG39 is a microtubular protein that may have an important role in cell proliferation, viral assembly/transport and/or microtubule dynamic.

the host response to JEV infection in the mouse brain is characterized by induction of genes that are also activated by Sindbis virus infection, and that the GARG39 protein is a novel microtubule associated protein that may have an important role in viral replication and/or cell proliferation.
the host response to JEV infection is not unique to JEV, but shares common features with Sindbis virus.
